newsitem.title: UK: Key UK cities miss out on job creation - survey.
newsitem.headline: Key UK cities miss out on job creation - survey.

text.p: British unemployment may be tumbling fast but several key cities fell behind over the last decade, Business Strategies said on Monday.
The leading business consultancy said job creation in Liverpool, Glasgow, Manchester, Portsmouth and Swansea had been "particularly disappointing."
The survey calculated what would have happened to employment in 50 cities across Britain if the dominant industries in those cities had created jobs at the same rate as they have done nationwide.
"In Liverpool, for example, employment should have risen by 9,000 between 1981 and 1993, given the industries the city has," said Richard Holt, director at Business Strategies.
Liverpool, once Britain's most successful seaport city, was hit hard in the 1980s as the structural decline of its key industries bit hard.
Even so, Holt said it was surprising that employment in the northwestern city fell by 64,000 in the 12 years to 1993.
"That is what we need to explain," Holt said. "Understanding why some places have done well will help the less successful take action to lift their future performance."
Nationally, unemployment is now running at 6.5 percent, its lowest level in six years. Back in 1993, the end of the survey period, it was running at 10 percent.

Holt contrasted Liverpool with the city of Exeter, in the heart of rural south-west of England. There, employment rose by 23 percent over the 12-year period but given its industrial mix, only a seven percent increase would have been expected.
"Exeter is popular because of its perceived high quality of life," Holt said.
But to put the jobs gap down to the north/south divide, the 1980s phenomenon which split generally affluent southerners from their less well-off northern counterparts, is too simple.
Towns such as Reading, situated in Britain's hi-tech industrial belt to the west of London, could reasonably have expected major employment growth, but has underachieved.
"People think places like Reading and Cambridge have done well in the past decade," Holt said. "Considering their industrial structure, what is surprising is that they did not do a lot better."
On the other hand, northern towns such as Leeds and Stockport actually did better than they were expected to.
